> **Key takeaways**
> - Run one party format, the same way every time: arrival, activity, food and cake, wrap-up.
> - Set a guest limit and an age range before you take a single booking.
> - Brief the host family a week ahead, and give every guest an easy way to find your classes.

## Why a birthday party program can work for a studio

Parents planning a birthday want two things: something the children will love, and someone else to run it. A studio, gym, art room or music school already has the space, the kit and people who know how to lead a group of kids.

A kids' birthday party at a studio also puts your activity in front of children and parents who may never have walked through your door. Done well, it introduces you to new families. Done badly, it is a long Saturday that eats your class time. The difference is planning.

## First, decide if parties fit your space and staff

Before you announce anything, answer a few honest questions:

- **Do you have a free slot?** Parties tend to land on weekends. A party only makes sense if it doesn't push a regular class out.
- **Can the room hold a group plus parents?** Some parents stay, some drop off. Picture the room with both.
- **Is there a place for food?** If food is allowed, you need a table and a floor you can clean fast. If not, say so up front.
- **Who will run it?** A party needs a lead plus at least one helper, without pulling anyone off a class.

Rules about food, room capacity and events can differ by city, landlord and activity. Check local rules and your own insurance and facility agreements before you offer parties.

## A simple party format

Pick one format and run it the same way every time, so families know what they're booking and your team knows what comes next:

1. **Arrival (about 15 minutes):** a simple warm-up game or station that works no matter when each guest walks in.
2. **The main activity (about 45 minutes):** your thing, led by your instructor. A short dance routine, a painting the kids take home, a mini obstacle course, a group song with instruments.
3. **Food and cake time (about 20 minutes), if allowed:** in a separate area if you have one, so the activity space stays clean.
4. **Wrap-up (about 10 minutes):** a quick show, a group photo the host takes, or handing out what the kids made. Then a calm pick-up.

A party of about 90 minutes is long enough to feel special and short enough to keep young kids happy.

## Group size and ages

Set a guest limit from your room, your kit and the hands-on help your activity needs. A painting party needs a seat and a canvas for every child; a gym party needs room to move safely.

Set an age range too: four-year-olds and ten-year-olds need different activities. If the guest list runs wider, plan for the youngest child in the room.

## What's included and what the host brings

Write down exactly what a party includes. For example:

- **Included:** the room for the full time, your instructor and helper, the activity and its materials, and any take-home item.
- **The host brings:** the cake, food and drinks (if allowed), plates and napkins, and any decorations you permit.
- **Not allowed:** say it plainly, whether that's glitter, confetti or candles.

Put the same list on your party page and in your confirmation message.

## Staffing the party

Good general practice:

- **One lead, one helper, minimum.** The lead runs the activity; the helper handles arrivals, bathroom trips and the food table.
- **Brief both before every party:** the birthday child's name and age, the guest count, any allergies the host shared, and the pick-up plan.
- **Assign one person to the door** at arrival and pick-up, and release each child only to the adult who dropped them off or one the parent named.

## Cleaning and turnaround

Parties end with crumbs and frosting on the floor. Plan for it:

- **Build a buffer of at least 30 minutes** between a party and your next class or party.
- **Keep a cleaning kit in the room:** wipes, a broom, bin bags and spare table covers.
- **Set a clear end time** with the host, and a gentle signal when it's ten minutes away.

## Booking windows and lead time

Parents plan parties around invitations and school calendars. Decide:

- **How far ahead you open dates.** Publishing two to three months of party slots lets parents plan around their child's birthday.
- **Your minimum lead time.** Asking for at least two weeks' notice gives you time to order materials and confirm staff.
- **Which slots you offer.** Fixed times, like Saturday and Sunday afternoons, are easier to staff than open requests.

## What to tell the host family beforehand

About a week before the party, send the host one clear message:

- **Time and place:** start and end times, the address, which door to use and where to park.
- **What's included** and what they bring.
- **Food rules** and where food and cake will happen.
- **Guest count and ages,** confirmed, with any allergies or support needs.
- **Signatures:** if you ask for waivers, whether you need one for every guest, not just the birthday child, and how to collect them before arrival.
- **Who to contact** on the day.

## Turning party guests into new families

Every guest is a child who just tried your activity, with a parent watching. Make the next step easy:

- **Send each guest home with something useful:** what they made, plus a small card with your class schedule and where to book.
- **Show your real classes at wrap-up.** A one-minute demo can do more than a flyer.
- **Let parents come to you.** Hand out the card and let interested parents reach out. Don't collect guests' contact details at the party.

## FAQ

### How long should a kids' birthday party at a studio be?
About 90 minutes suits most ages: arrival, a main activity, food and cake if allowed, and a calm wrap-up.

### How many guests should a studio party allow?
Base it on your room, your materials and the hands-on help the activity needs, and set it before you take bookings.

### Can families bring their own cake and food?
That is your call, based on your space and any local rules or agreements. If you allow it, say what is fine and where food happens.

### How far ahead should families book a party?
Ask for at least two weeks' notice, and open dates two to three months ahead so parents can plan.

### How can a party bring new families to my classes?
Send every guest home with what they made and a card with your class schedule, and show a short class demo at wrap-up.
